storyBody.heading: Production Sheets and the Halloween Slot
paragraphs: The story chain begins on the evening of October 30, 1938, when CBS scheduled the Mercury Theatre version of H. G. Wells’ *The War of the Worlds* in a standard radio-night slot. Internal program logs and cue sheets identified exact transition points: opening introduction, scripted drama scene, then a sequence of urgent-sounding bulletins. In short, the event starts as a normal broadcast operation with an internal chain of scheduling documents, actor cues, and announcer timing.

storyBody.heading: Scripted Bulletins Cut In as News
paragraphs: At the scheduled transition, the program switched into faux breaking-news segments that described a comet strike in New Jersey and moving emergency conditions. The audience heard the same language and tone as live reporting, not a theatrical warning frame. This was the key sequencing change: listeners who tuned in mid-program missed the disclaimer that it was fiction, so the call-sheeted cue became part of the perceived present tense.

storyBody.heading: Listener Confusion and the Station Call Log
paragraphs: Within minutes, stations received calls from listeners asking for clarifications, and local institutions were reported in newspaper columns as receiving urgent public questions. The incident was not a perfectly uniform mass panic, but a measurable chain: ambiguous on-air framing, uncertainty in the audience, then verification attempts through phone contact and desk-level response. That call log pressure turned the broadcast into an event record, because each incoming report fed the idea that the broadcast had crossed into public emergency context.

storyBody.heading: Print Coverage and Broadcast Aftershocks
paragraphs: The next step was immediate amplification. Morning papers and rival network commentators repeated the event as a cautionary example of media authority and realism. As stories repeated, the original production cue sequence was compressed into a simpler warning formula: fake bulletins can turn entertainment into panic when timing and trust collapse. The incident therefore moved from one studio broadcast to a lesson-shaped narrative repeated in journalism, media studies, and radio history.
